plants.name: Hydrangea
plants.pph_toxicity_note: All parts of the Hydrangea plant contain cyanide-containing compounds. When the plant material is chewed or damaged (e.g., frost, crushing) free cyanide can be released triggering cyanide poisoning when ingested. Cyanide reduces the body’s ability to process oxygen at a cellular level resulting in clinical signs including vomiting, drooling, gasping, collapse, seizure, and death. The occurrence of cyanide poisoning from ingestion of this plant is higher in livestock – animals that consume large amounts and chew their food well – vs. companion animals.

plants.name: Heavenly Bamboo
plants.pph_toxicity_note: All parts of Heavenly Bamboo may contain cyanide-containing compounds and enzymes. When the plant material is chewed or damaged (e.g., frost, crushing) free cyanide can be released triggering cyanide poisoning when ingested. Cyanide reduces the body’s ability to process oxygen at a cellular level resulting in clinical signs including vomiting, drooling, gasping, collapse, seizure, and death. When pets chew the plant, it releases the crystals causing irritation and pain to the pet’s lips, oral cavity, and throat. Drooling, gagging, and vomiting are common signs in animals following ingestion of this plant; in rare instances severe throat swelling resulting in breathing difficulty can occur.

plants.name: Weeping Fig
plants.pph_toxicity_note: Weeping fig is one common name for Ficus benjamina. Numerous species of plants belong to the genus Ficus and contain irritating sap. Following ingestion, irritation of the mouth and gastrointestinal tract may occur. Dermal irritation is also possible if the sap gets on the pet’s skin. Common signs to watch for: Decreased appetite Drooling Vomiting Diarrhea Skin irritation

plants.name: Yucca
plants.pph_toxicity_note: The yucca plant, which commonly grows in warm climates, contains steroidal saponins. In dogs and cats, it typically causes only mild vomiting and diarrhea and possibly pupil dilation. In grazing animals who may chronically ingest it, this plant may also cause liver and kidney signs. The sharp points on the leaves may cause mechanical injury to skin or GI tract.

plants.pph_toxicity_note: Grazing livestock that consume large amounts of delphinium develop nervous system signs of weakness and stumbling gait plus bloating, difficulty breathing, and death. Because dogs and cats usually ingest much smaller amounts of delphinium their signs are milder and include lethargy, vomiting, and diarrhea.

Ingestion of several leaves/ seeds of Euonymus by companion animals commonly results in stomach upset; however, irregular heart rhythm and collapse may occur following a massive ingestion.

Ingestion of iris – especially the rhizome- can result in drooling, vomiting, diarrhea, and lethargy in pets.

plants.name: Rhododendron
plants.pph_toxicity_note: Rhododendrons contain grayanotoxins within all parts of the plant. Ingestion of rhododendron by animals results in gastrointestinal distress (e.g., vomiting, hypersalivation, drooling, colic), cardiovascular abnormalities (e.g., heart rhythm irregularity, low blood pressure), and neurological signs (e.g., depression, seizure). Severe clinical signs are expected with large ingestion (e.g., grazing by goats or cattle) but also may occur in cats or dogs that consume only a few leaves or flowers.

plants.name: Daphne
plants.pph_toxicity_note: Foliage, bark and berries of Daphne contain irritant toxins. Ocular or oral contact with this plant leads to blistering, redness, and swelling of eyes, mouth, or stomach/intestines. Vomiting and diarrhea – sometimes with blood – may also occur. Daphne is toxic to companion animals (dogs and cats) and livestock.

plants.name: Lupin
plants.pph_toxicity_note: Specific wild lupines contain the alkaloid toxin anagyrine. Ingestion of seeds/ seed pods by grazing livestock during pregnancy results in fetal birth defects; sheep are the most sensitive and goats the most resistant to this toxin. Other clinical signs reported in livestock grazing wild lupine seeds/ seed pods includes sudden respiratory failure and liver disease.
